services.name: Drain Cleaning
services.h1: Drain Cleaning in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Drains | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock clears slow, backed-up, and odorous drains in Round Rock, TX, with fixture checks, cable clearing, and camera follow-up when needed.
services.blurb: Clearing slow, gurgling, backed-up, and odorous drains across Round Rock.

paragraphs: A sink that gurgles after the faucet stops, a shower that holds water around your feet, or a floor drain with a sewer smell usually points to a blockage somewhere beyond the fixture. We check the basin, trap, drain opening, and visible pipe route to tell whether the restriction is close to the room or farther along the line.

Hair, soap residue, grease, food scraps, and paper can collect in different parts of a drain pipe. We clear the blockage without treating every slow fixture as the same problem, because a bathroom sink, kitchen line, and floor drain can each have a different route and access point. A mildly slow sink may wait briefly if water still drains, but repeated backup, a floor drain filling, or wastewater rising in a tub should not wait because the blockage can overflow into the room and spread farther through the pipe.

sections.heading: Gurgling sinks and floor drains
paragraphs: We often hear about a kitchen sink that drains slowly until the dishwasher runs, a shower pan that fills before the water is shut off, or a toilet that makes nearby sink water bubble. A gurgling sound can mean air is being displaced by water around a restriction, while standing water in a tub may indicate that the blockage is lower in the shared branch pipe.

We also get calls about a rotten smell from a floor drain, water coming back through a laundry drain, and a basin that empties only after plunging. Grease at a kitchen trap, hair around a stopper, scale inside an older pipe, or debris farther down the line can produce similar symptoms. We inspect the fixture and pipe route before recommending work, since these faults can look alike from the room but require different equipment, access, and cost.

sections.heading: Drain inspection and clearing
paragraphs: We start the visit by running water at the affected fixture, checking the stopper or strainer, and looking at the trap, cleanout, and exposed drain pipe. A basic fixture check commonly takes about 10 to 15 minutes. Sink and tub branches are often smaller than a main drain, so we match the cable and cutting head to the opening and pipe rather than forcing a large tool through a narrow fixture line.

Where the blockage is reachable, we can usually remove debris from a stopper, clean a trap, or cable-clear a branch on the same visit; a typical fixture-level cable clearing may take 30 to 60 minutes depending on the buildup and pipe bends. If flow does not return, we may use a camera to look for roots, a break, heavy scale, or an offset joint farther along the route. A camera inspection can add another 30 to 60 minutes, while work requiring access behind a wall, beneath a slab, or farther outside the building is normally arranged as a separate visit. If a damaged strainer, stopper, trap washer, or cleanout cap is found, we explain the part before replacement.

sections.heading: Pipe route and cleanout access
paragraphs: The pipe route, the access point, and the pipe material are major factors in the scope of drain work. A clog at a sink trap under a cabinet is different from a blockage reached through a floor cleanout, roof vent, or exterior access point. PVC, cast iron, galvanized steel, and older mixed pipe runs can each affect how we approach the line and which cable head or camera setup is appropriate.

Heavy grease, compacted paper, tree roots, mineral scale, and a collapsed section do not clear in the same way. Cabinets packed around a trap, a painted-over cleanout cap, or a cap that has seized can add preparation and may require a replacement fitting. We also account for whether the affected drain serves a single fixture or several rooms, and whether access through a tenant space, utility room, or exterior gate needs approval before the line can be checked.

sections.heading: Fixture and cleanout location
paragraphs: Before calling, note which fixture is slow or backed up and which room it is in, such as the kitchen sink, hall bathroom tub, laundry standpipe, or garage floor drain. Tell us whether water is standing now, whether another fixture bubbles when water runs, and whether the problem began after grease, wipes, food, or another item entered the drain.

If you can safely see a cleanout cap, let us know whether it is under a sink, in a utility room, outside near the foundation, or at a floor drain. A photo of the sink cabinet, trap, or access opening can help us plan the cable and camera equipment. Avoid pouring chemical cleaner into the pipe before we arrive, since the liquid can remain in the trap and create a hazard around the drain opening. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before a slow fixture turns into wastewater backing up through a tub, sink, or floor drain.

services.name: Water Heater Repair
services.h1: Water Heater Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Water Heater Repair | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles water heater repair in Round Rock, TX, checking leaks, burners, thermostats, tanks, and hot-water recovery issues.
services.blurb: Tank, burner, thermostat, and leak checks for water heaters in Round Rock.

paragraphs: A water heater that rumbles behind a utility-room door but delivers only lukewarm water is not the same job as a heater leaving a wet trail from the closet or garage into the hallway. The first problem usually shows at the shower or kitchen tap; the second shows up as water at the base, a dripping relief pipe, or a soaked drain pan. We diagnose and repair both tank and tankless units, tracing the symptom back to the heater rather than treating every complaint as the same failure.

Hot water that fades during a shower can come from a worn heating element, a thermostat, sediment at the bottom of a tank, an undersized burner flame, or a tankless unit that is shutting down mid-cycle. Water around the heater can come from a loose supply connection, the temperature-pressure relief valve, a corroded fitting, a leaking drain valve, or the tank itself. We check the appliance, its water connections, the vent or electrical supply, and the discharge piping before recommending a repair.

A loss of hot water without a leak can sometimes wait until the heater can be inspected, provided there is no gas odor, burning smell, tripped breaker, or water escaping from the unit. Water at the tank base, a leaking relief line, or a burner that will not operate safely should not wait, because continued water flow can damage flooring and a fuel or electrical fault can affect the heater’s safe operation.

sections.heading: No hot water or puddles
paragraphs: Calls often start with “no hot water,” “the shower goes cold,” “the water heater is making a popping noise,” or “there is a puddle under the tank.” A pilot that will not stay lit on a gas heater points to a different set of parts than an electric heater with a reset button that keeps tripping. Rust-colored water from several hot taps may involve tank corrosion or an aging anode rod, while a steady drip from the pipe outside the heater may be coming from the relief valve instead of the tank. A sulfur-like smell, a burner that clicks without lighting, or a display showing an error code gives us another useful starting point. These symptoms can sound alike from across a room, but they lead to different failed parts, repair steps, and job costs once we inspect the heater.

sections.heading: Tank and burner inspection
paragraphs: During an inspection, we start at the model plate and identify whether the unit is gas, electric, or tankless, then check the age, capacity, fuel connection, shutoff valve, venting, electrical supply, and visible piping. We look for moisture at the cold-water inlet, hot-water outlet, drain valve, relief valve, expansion tank, and the seam around the tank jacket. On a gas unit, we inspect the burner compartment, ignition components, pilot assembly where fitted, combustion air openings, and vent pipe. On an electric unit, we test the thermostat, upper and lower elements, wiring terminals, and reset control; many residential electric tanks operate on a 240-volt circuit.

A first inspection and basic testing commonly takes about 20 to 40 minutes, although a concealed heater closet, an active leak, or a tankless error code can add time. If the fault is an accessible thermostat, heating element, thermocouple, ignition part, relief valve, or supply connector, we can often complete the repair on the same visit when the required part is available. A corroded tank, a damaged vent route, a seized shutoff, a replacement unit, or a control board that must be ordered may require a separate scheduled installation or return visit.

sections.heading: Anodes, shutoffs and access
paragraphs: The age and condition of the heater matter because a replaceable heating element or thermostat is a different repair from corrosion through the tank wall. An anode rod that has worn down can contribute to rust and odor issues, while a tank that is leaking from its body generally needs replacement rather than a new external fitting. The model, fuel type, and availability of the required burner assembly, element, thermostat, or control board also affect the scope of the work.

Access changes the job as well. A heater in an open garage is usually simpler to inspect than a unit behind shelving, in a tight closet, on an elevated platform, or connected to rigid pipe with little room around the shutoff valve. If the water shutoff has seized, the supply lines are corroded, or the drain valve will not open, additional work may be needed before the failed component can be removed. When replacement affects gas piping, venting, electrical connections, or local permit requirements, any required inspection or sign-off also becomes part of planning the work.

sections.heading: Model plate and access panel
paragraphs: Before calling, check the model number and serial number on the manufacturer’s plate, which is commonly attached to the side of a tank or behind an access panel on a tankless unit. Let us know whether the heater is in a garage, attic, closet, utility room, or exterior enclosure, and whether there is clear access to the front panel and water shutoff. The approximate installation age, the fuel type, and any error code or flashing light on the display can help us identify likely parts. If water is running now, note whether it is coming from the top connections, the relief pipe, the drain valve, or the bottom of the tank. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790, because water escaping from a heater can continue into drywall, flooring, and the subfloor while the leak remains active.

services.name: Leak Repair
services.h1: Leak Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Leak Repair - Plumbing Solutions Round Rock - Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles leak repair in Round Rock, TX, including dripping faucets, wet cabinets, pipe joints, and hidden water damage.
services.blurb: Leak repair for dripping fixtures, wet cabinets, and pipe joints in Round Rock.

paragraphs: A drip from a faucet can seem minor until the sink cabinet stays damp, the wood swells around the supply valve, or water reaches the floor beneath it. A pinhole in a copper line may leave only a small stain at first, then spread moisture through drywall, baseboards, insulation, or a ceiling below. The longer water travels behind a wall or under a vanity, the harder it is to see where the original leak began.

A leak can also change with the season and with daily water use. A loose compression nut may only seep while a faucet runs, while a failed toilet supply line or refrigerator line can keep feeding water into a cabinet even when nobody is using the fixture. Mineral buildup around a valve stem, a wet ring below a pipe joint, and a water meter that moves when fixtures are off can all point to water leaving the plumbing system.

An active leak, a wet ceiling, a soft cabinet floor, or water near an electrical outlet should not wait because the water is already reaching building materials beyond the fitting itself. A contained faucet drip may be scheduled, but we still recommend repair before the washer, cartridge, or valve body creates damage around the fixture.

sections.heading: Dripping faucets and wet cabinets
paragraphs: Customers often call us about a faucet that will not stop dripping, a sink cabinet with water under the pipes, or a puddle that returns after the cabinet has been dried. A drip at the spout can come from a worn cartridge, a damaged washer, or a valve seat, while water around the base of the faucet can be coming from a loose mounting nut, failed gasket, or a supply connection under the counter.

A hissing sound behind drywall, a brown spot on a ceiling, peeling paint near a shower wall, or a warm patch on a floor can indicate a concealed water line leak. Some customers notice a musty smell in a vanity cabinet, while others see the water meter continue to move after faucets, ice makers, and other fixtures are shut off.

Water around an angle stop, corrosion on a braided supply line, and a damp pipe joint can look alike from the front of a cabinet. These symptoms can come from separate parts and require different repairs, so we inspect the connection and water path before tying the work to a particular part or repair scope.

sections.heading: Fixture and pipe inspection
paragraphs: We start by locating the wet area and tracing the water path back to the fixture, valve, supply line, drain connection, or pipe joint. We check visible fittings with a light, inspect cabinet panels and drywall with a moisture meter, and run the affected fixture to see whether the leak appears during use, after use, or continuously. Where the leak is not visible, we can isolate fixtures and use the water meter or a pressure gauge to narrow down the source.

A typical residential water supply is commonly regulated between 40 and 80 psi, and unusually high pressure can stress faucet cartridges, supply hoses, and shutoff valves. For a suspected hidden supply leak, an isolated pressure test may be watched for 15 minutes or longer while fixtures remain off. An accessible faucet, trap connection, or under-sink supply line can often be checked in 30 to 60 minutes, although damp drywall or a concealed pipe can require additional tracing.

On the same visit, we can commonly replace exposed washers, cartridges, supply lines, escutcheons, or leaking compression fittings when the correct part is available and the connection is accessible. A pipe behind tile, inside a wall, under a slab, or behind a built-in cabinet may need an access opening, a specialty fitting, or a follow-up visit after parts are obtained. We explain which pipe or fitting is leaking before work moves beyond the visible area.

sections.heading: Shutoff valves and wall access
paragraphs: The condition of the shutoff valve and the route to the leak are major factors in the repair scope. A supply line connected to a working angle stop inside an open sink cabinet is different from a line whose shutoff has seized, whose packing nut is corroded, or whose valve must be replaced before the leaking connection can be safely worked on. Water may need to be isolated at another valve when the local shutoff will not close.

Wall access also changes the work involved. A leak at an exposed PEX, copper, or PVC joint can be repaired directly, while a pipe behind tile, plaster, a shower enclosure, cabinetry, or insulation may require a careful opening and later surface repair by the appropriate trade. The age and material of the fitting matter because older valves, galvanized pipe, discontinued faucet cartridges, and specialty hose connections can need ordered parts rather than a standard replacement.

We also account for whether the leak has affected a shared wall, a ceiling cavity, or a location where building approval or property management sign-off is required. A clearly visible fitting with open access is generally more straightforward than a concealed line with damaged material around it, and we discuss those conditions before expanding the repair.

sections.heading: Fixture room and valve model
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room and fixture are involved, such as the kitchen sink, upstairs bathroom vanity, shower valve, laundry box, or exterior hose bib. If the faucet or shower trim has a brand name or model marking on the handle, escutcheon plate, spout, or underside of the fixture, that marking can help us identify the cartridge or replacement part.

Tell us whether water is running now, whether the leak only appears while the fixture is on, and whether the local shutoff valve closes. A photo of the wet cabinet, supply hose, pipe joint, or ceiling stain can show the access around the fitting before we arrive.

If the fixture was installed recently or has an approximate age, include that with the location of any access panel, crawlspace entry, or wall opening. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before a wet cabinet, ceiling stain, or pipe joint allows water to spread farther into drywall and framing.

services.name: Toilet Repair
services.h1: Toilet Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Toilets | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: At Plumbing Solutions Round Rock, we repair toilets in Round Rock, TX, including running tanks, weak flushes, and leaks at the base. Call (737) 405-5790.
services.blurb: We repair running toilets, weak flushes, tank leaks, and loose toilet bases.

paragraphs: A handle jiggle, a quick plunge, or lifting the tank lid to free a snagged chain is a sensible first response when a toilet will not stop running or will not flush. Those small checks can reseat a flapper, clear a little paper from the bowl, or put the lift chain back on its hook. They stop helping when the rubber seal is warped, the fill valve is sticking, the flush valve seat is worn, or the bowl has a blockage farther along than a plunger can reach.

We repair toilet faults in Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch by checking the tank, bowl, shutoff, supply tube, base, and drain connection instead of guessing at one visible symptom. A toilet that runs occasionally can sometimes wait for a planned repair if the water stays inside the tank and the shutoff valve works. Water at the base, a cracked tank, a bowl that rises toward the rim, or an overflow tube that runs continuously should not wait, because those faults can damage flooring, waste water, or turn into an overflow.

sections.heading: Toilet keeps running
paragraphs: We often hear that “the toilet keeps running,” “it hisses after flushing,” “the handle does nothing,” or “it flushes but the bowl barely clears.” A running sound may come from a flapper that no longer seals, a fill valve that will not shut off, or water escaping through the overflow tube. A weak flush can come from low tank water, a kinked lift chain, clogged rim holes, a worn flush valve, or a partial blockage in the trapway.

Other calls start with water around the toilet base, a tank that refills by itself, a toilet that rocks on the floor, or a sewer smell near the bowl. A wet floor may be condensation, a loose supply connection, leaking tank bolts, or a failed wax ring below the fixture. These faults can look similar from outside the tank, but they require different parts and different amounts of work once we inspect the toilet.

sections.heading: Tank and bowl inspection
paragraphs: We begin the inspection at the shutoff valve and supply tube, then remove the tank lid and flush the toilet several times. We check the chain length, flapper or canister seal, fill valve, overflow tube, tank water level, handle arm, tank bolts, and the condition of the porcelain. If the fill valve is not behaving normally, we can check incoming water pressure with a gauge; residential plumbing commonly operates between 40 and 80 psi. We also check whether the toilet uses a 2-inch or 3-inch flush valve, since the wrong flapper size will not seal properly.

A typical diagnostic check takes about 20 to 40 minutes, depending on access around the toilet and whether the fault appears on every flush. Straightforward work such as replacing a flapper, fill valve, handle, supply tube, or tank bolts is usually completed during the same visit and often takes 45 to 90 minutes. If we find a cracked bowl, damaged closet flange, floor movement around the base, or a discontinued tank component, we may need to order the correct part or book return work after the fixture and floor connection have been assessed.

sections.heading: Fill valve and shutoff
paragraphs: The age and type of the tank parts affect the repair scope. A common fill valve or flapper can be replaced without removing the toilet, while an older proprietary flush assembly may require a matching seal, tower, or tank component. Access also matters: a toilet tight against a wall, boxed-in supply line, corroded tank bolts, or flooring built up around the base can add removal and reinstallation work.

The shutoff valve is another important factor. If the valve turns freely and stops the water, we can isolate the toilet while we work; if it has seized, leaks at the stem, or will not close completely, that issue may need attention before tank parts can be changed. A part that must be ordered, approval from an owner or building manager, or a damaged flange below the bowl can also move the repair beyond a simple tank adjustment.

sections.heading: Tank model and bathroom
paragraphs: Before calling, check which bathroom has the problem and whether the toilet is running, leaking, or backing up right now. If you can safely lift the tank lid, look for a brand name and any model number molded or stamped inside the tank or on the underside of the lid. Let us know whether the fixture is an older toilet, a dual-flush model, or a toilet with a push button instead of a handle. It also helps to mention tight cabinet access, tile around the base, or water damage on the floor near the bowl. Call (737) 405-5790 with those tank and bathroom details, because a running toilet or base leak can worsen the water damage beneath the fixture if it waits.

services.name: Sewer Line Repair
services.h1: Sewer Line Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Sewer Repair | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock, Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles sewer line repair in Round Rock, TX, with camera inspection, locating, repair planning, and clear next steps for backups.
services.blurb: Camera-led sewer line checks and repair planning for backups, odors, and slow fixtures.

paragraphs: We hear from homeowners and property managers when “everything is backing up,” “the shower drain is bubbling,” or “it smells like sewage outside.” Those are the words people use because the trouble often shows up first at a toilet bowl, tub drain, shower, or floor drain rather than at the buried pipe itself. We translate the symptom into a sewer-line check, looking for a blockage, root intrusion, cracked pipe, separated joint, or a line that no longer has a clear route to the connection.

A single slow sink can be limited to one fixture, but water rising in a shower drain when another fixture runs points further down the system. We work across Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch to inspect the line and identify the section that needs attention. A sewer backup should not wait, because wastewater can come through low drains, soak flooring and wall materials, and continue forcing solids into a damaged or blocked pipe.

sections.heading: Sewage smell and gurgling
paragraphs: People commonly call when a toilet bubbles after the washing machine drains, a shower pan fills with murky water, or several drains slow down at once. A sewage smell near the yard, cleanout, or bathroom can also indicate a loose cap, leaking joint, or a buried line that is allowing wastewater to escape. Another frequent report is a wet strip of ground above the pipe route, especially when the soil stays damp without recent rain.

A gurgling bowl can come from restricted flow, while water at a shower drain may mean the main line cannot carry discharge away. Roots entering a joint, scale inside older cast-iron pipe, a belly in the line, and a collapsed section can all create similar household symptoms. These complaints sound alike from inside the home, but the pipe fault, repair method, materials, and work involved can be very different once we inspect the route.

sections.heading: Camera inspection and locating
paragraphs: At the visit, we start with the accessible cleanout, drain openings, and the fixtures affected by the backup. We check whether water is standing in the pipe, whether the cleanout cap can be removed safely, and whether flow changes when a fixture is used. A camera inspection sends a flexible cable through the line, while a transmitter helps us trace the pipe route from above ground. A straightforward camera pass commonly takes about fifteen to thirty minutes; tracing a long route, locating an underground defect, or working through limited access can take longer.

The camera shows the pipe material, joint condition, root growth, offset connections, cracks, and the approximate location of a restriction. Residential building drains are often three or four inches in diameter, and that measurement matters when planning a replacement fitting or pipe section. When a cracked cleanout riser, cap, or exposed pipe section is accessible, we may be able to replace it during the same visit. Excavation, replacement of a longer buried run, restoration of concrete or landscaping, and any repair requiring permit review are typically planned as follow-up work after the line location and scope are clear.

sections.heading: Pipe depth and access
paragraphs: Pipe depth and access change the scope of a sewer repair more than the symptom inside the bathroom. A defect beneath open soil beside a driveway is different from one beneath a concrete slab, patio, fence line, mature tree, or utility route. We also consider whether the cleanout provides a usable entry point, whether the pipe can be reached from the yard, and whether wastewater must be controlled before work begins.

The pipe material and failure type matter as well. Root intrusion at a joint, a split in plastic pipe, corrosion in cast iron, and a crushed section each call for different fittings and repair methods. A line with a known route and an accessible damaged section is generally more direct to plan than a buried route that needs locating, excavation, ordered material, or local permit and inspection sign-off.

sections.heading: Cleanout location and pipe material
paragraphs: Before calling, we can use the location of the cleanout and the room where the backup first appeared to plan the inspection. The cleanout is often a capped pipe near an exterior wall, foundation, or yard line; please do not force a cap that is stuck or surrounded by standing wastewater. If you know whether the pipe is cast iron, PVC, ABS, or clay, tell us, and mention any prior excavation, patch, or visible pipe section.

We also need to know which fixtures are backing up, whether water is currently standing in a shower, tub, or floor drain, and whether the yard, crawlspace, driveway, or gate provides access to the suspected route. Photos of the cleanout, wet ground, or exposed pipe can help us understand the layout before the visit. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790, because a restricted sewer line can progress from gurgling fixtures to wastewater backing up through the lowest drain.

services.name: Garbage Disposal Repair
services.h1: Garbage Disposal Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Disposal Repair | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock repairs jammed, humming, leaking garbage disposals in Round Rock, TX, Brushy Creek, Windemere, Wells Branch, and nearby kitchens.
services.blurb: We repair jammed, humming, leaking garbage disposals across Round Rock.

paragraphs: In older Round Rock homes, the disposal, sink flange, drain collar, and dishwasher hose have often been in the same cabinet for years. Moisture around a metal mounting ring can leave it corroded, while food residue and mineral buildup can make the grinding chamber harder to turn. In apartments and newer kitchens around Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch, a disposal problem may instead show up after a utensil, bottle cap, or fibrous food catches beneath the impellers.

We check the disposal as part of the whole under-sink assembly, including the power connection, wall switch, reset button, splash guard, mounting hardware, drain outlet, and dishwasher connection where fitted. A disposal can sound like an appliance problem when the obstruction is in the grinding chamber, but water at the cabinet floor may come from the sink flange, discharge elbow, or dishwasher hose rather than the motor housing.

A humming disposal with a dry cabinet can usually be left switched off until we inspect it. Water under the sink, a burning electrical smell, repeated breaker trips, or standing sink water should not be left in use, because a stalled motor can overheat and a cabinet leak can damage the base, flooring, and electrical connection.

sections.heading: Humming motor and sink water
paragraphs: A common call starts with a hum when the wall switch is on, but the grinding plate does not turn. Another is a disposal that makes a hard rattle or clanking noise after a fork, bone fragment, screw, or piece of glass has entered the chamber. We also hear about a sink that fills when the disposal runs, a reset button that keeps popping out, and a sour odor that remains even after the sink has been rinsed.

Water can drip from the bottom of the disposal body, the metal mounting ring, the black drain elbow, or the dishwasher hose connection. A unit that is completely silent may have a switch, receptacle, reset, wiring, or motor issue, while a unit that runs but leaves food in the sink may have a jammed plate or restricted outlet. Those symptoms can look alike from above the sink, but they point to different parts and different repair work once we inspect the cabinet and disposal.

sections.heading: Disposal callout and testing
paragraphs: On a disposal callout, we first isolate the power at the switch or breaker and inspect the cabinet for water, loose wiring, damaged insulation, and movement at the sink flange. We check the reset button, turn the grinding plate by hand with the proper tool when the unit is de-energized, and look inside the chamber for metal, plastic, or food debris. We also test the wall switch and receptacle, check for a 120-volt supply where applicable, and run water through the drain outlet and dishwasher inlet to locate a leak.

A basic jam check, reset test, and mounting inspection commonly takes minutes; removing a lodged object or replacing a splash guard, discharge gasket, drain elbow, or mounting hardware can often be handled during the same visit when the matching part is available. If the motor has seized, the housing has cracked, the mounting system is discontinued, or a compatible replacement disposal must be ordered, we explain the next step before fitting anything. Electrical circuit repairs, cabinet alterations, and work requiring a specific replacement unit may need a separate booking.

sections.heading: Mounting ring and cabinet access
paragraphs: The condition of the mounting ring and sink flange can change the scope of a disposal repair. A newer unit with a loose drain elbow or worn gasket is usually more direct to open up than an older disposal with rusted mounting tabs, hardened putty at the flange, or a corroded discharge connection. If the motor or lower housing has failed, the make, mounting pattern, and existing drain layout determine whether a replacement can connect without changing the pipework.

Cabinet access matters as well. Cleaning products, pullout shelves, water filters, and crowded dishwasher hoses can limit room around the disposal and drain trap. A part that matches the existing unit can be fitted more simply than a discontinued collar, specialty splash guard, or replacement disposal that has to be ordered. We also allow for any electrical or kitchen fixture requirements that apply when the work extends beyond the disposal assembly.

sections.heading: Model plate and sink cabinet
paragraphs: Before calling, check the label or model plate on the side or underside of the disposal, where the make and model are often printed. Let us know which kitchen sink has the issue, whether the unit hums, leaks, runs continuously, or trips the reset button, and whether water is standing in the basin.

If you know when the disposal was installed, that can help identify an older mounting system or discontinued part. Clear a path to the sink cabinet if possible, and mention any water filter, pullout bin, dishwasher hose, or shelving beside the drain. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before a leak beneath the disposal swells the cabinet base or reaches the electrical connection.
